candidate.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items), within Physiological Integrity; this item tests a nonpharmacologic comfort and breathing-support intervention used to reduce respiratory distress.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Nonpharmacologic breathing technique for comfort and symptom control in obstructive lung disease
candidate.educational_objective: Teach pursed-lip breathing as a supportive COPD breathing technique that prolongs controlled exhalation, creates slight expiratory backpressure, reduces air trapping and work of breathing, and can lessen dyspnea without replacing prescribed therapy.

options.A: Slow exhalation through pursed lips prolongs expiration and creates slight expiratory backpressure that can reduce air trapping and the sensation of dyspnea
options.B: The technique works mainly by causing rapid shallow breathing and shortening the expiratory phase
options.C: Pursed-lip breathing replaces prescribed bronchodilator therapy when COPD symptoms increase
options.D: The technique intentionally promotes small-airway collapse during exhalation so trapped air remains in the lungs

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI/StatPearls guidance describes pursed-lip breathing as a slow, controlled exhalation through pursed lips that prolongs the expiratory phase and generates a small amount of positive expiratory pressure. This backpressure helps resist airway collapse, supports more complete exhalation, reduces air trapping, decreases work of breathing, and can relieve dyspnea. B and D describe the opposite of the intended expiratory mechanics. C is incorrect because pursed-lip breathing is a supportive nonpharmacologic technique and does not replace prescribed COPD medications. The final item does not claim a universal improvement in exercise tolerance because response to the technique can vary by population and clinical context.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports prolonged controlled exhalation, slight expiratory backpressure, reduced airway collapse/air trapping, reduced work of breathing, and dyspnea relief as the pursed-lip-breathing construct tested by the item.
candidate.source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Pursed-lip Breathing' → Definition/Introduction: deliberate nasal inhalation followed by slow controlled exhalation through pursed lips prolongs expiration and generates a small amount of positive end-expiratory pressure; the backpressure helps prevent airway collapse and reduces air trapping. Clinical Significance: pursed-lip breathing can reduce work of breathing and alleviate dyspnea; effectiveness varies across patient populations, supporting individualized use rather than a universal functional-outcome claim.
candidate.source_version_date: StatPearls; last update 2025-01-25; current 2026 NCBI Bookshelf edition accessed 2026-08-18
candidate.stem: A nurse teaches a client with COPD to use pursed-lip breathing during episodes of breathlessness. Which explanation of the technique is accurate?
